chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Sadeer entered upon my father (peace be upon him) in the month of Ramadan and he said: 'O Sadeer, do you know which nights these are?' He said: 'Yes, my father, may I be your ransom, these are the nights of the month of Ramadan.' He said to him: 'What then?' He said to him: 'Can you afford to free ten slaves from the descendants of Ismail every night?' Sadeer said to him: 'My father and mother be my ransom, my wealth does not reach that.' He kept reducing the number until he reached one slave, and Sadeer kept saying 'I cannot afford that.' He said to him: 'Then can you afford to break the fast with a Muslim man every night?' He said: 'Yes, and ten.' He said to him: 'That is what I meant, O Sadeer. Your breaking the fast with your Muslim brother is equivalent to freeing one slave from the descendants of Ismail.'

key_terms.إِفْطَارُكَ: your breaking the fast (hosting for iftar)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual equivalent of freeing a slave according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) guides Sadeer to prioritize accessible acts of worship by equating the reward of hosting a Muslim for iftar to that of freeing a slave from the descendants of Ismail. This comparison highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on social solidarity and the practicality of charity, ensuring that spiritual merit is not limited by financial capacity. The narration underscores the high status of feeding the fasting believer as a direct substitute for the historically significant act of manumission.
